## Main Message

By assaying thermal limits several times per year in natural populations distributed across a large latitudinal gradient, we highlight the importance of intra-specific variation for predicting vulnerability to climate change. Indeed, across the entire spatiotemporal framework examined here, we observed an \~12°C range in thermal limits. Both spatial and temporal variations in thermal limits are essential for robust predictions. Also highlighted in this study are the major differences in thermal limits between the various cryptic lineages of *Acartia tonsa*. The broad (and sometimes overlapping) distrbutions of these clades provide a unique opportunity to compare replicate spatiotemporal patterns in adaptation against a relatively similar genetic background.

## 1. Collections and environment

Collection sites, conditions at the time of collection, continuous temperature records, and the timing of collections relative to copepod generation times.

### Sites and collection conditions

Copepods were collected by surface tow from sites across the Western Atlantic at several times throughout the year. The sites are shown below along with surface temperatures and salinity were measured at the time of collection. Across the entire set of collections, temperature ranged from `r min(site_temps$collection_temp)`°C to `r max(site_temps$collection_temp)`°C.

```{r}
#| label: site-chars
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
coords = site_data %>%
  dplyr::select(site, long, lat) %>%
  distinct() %>% 
  filter(site != "Key Largo")

site_map = map_data("world") %>% 
  filter(region %in% c("USA", "Canada")) %>% 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_polygon(aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = "lightgrey") + 
  coord_map(xlim = c(-85,-60),
            ylim = c(25, 48)) + 
  geom_point(data = coords,
             mapping = aes(x = long, y = lat, colour = site),
             size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_cols) + 
  labs(x = "Longitude", 
       y = "Latitude") + 
  theme_matt(base_size = 16)

site_temp_plot = ggplot(site_temps, aes(x = doy, y = collection_temp, colour = site)) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 2) + 
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_cols) + 
  labs(y = "Temperature (°C)",
       x = "Day of the Year") +
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "right")

ggarrange(site_map, site_temp_plot, common.legend = T, legend = "bottom")
```

Collections aimed to obtain copepods near the onset of peak temperatures, after peak temperatures, and then after temperatures cooled during the Fall. To put the collections into this larger seasonal context, we examined continuous temperature records for each site. Continuous data is not available for all sites, however, so here we've pieced together daily temperature values from either local temperature sensors (sites in Florida and the Chesapeake) and high resolution satellite temperature data (Connecticut, Maine, and the Canadian sites). This satellite data comes from the NOAA 1/4° Daily Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature (OISST).

These temperature profiles are shown below, with the temperatures measured during the time of collection included for comparison While collection temperatures in Maine did not always match the recorded daily averages, across all sites the temperature records do give a general sense of the timing of seasonal maxima (and the proximity of collections to the seasonal maximum temperature). In general, the first sample from each site fell just after the site reached the warmest period. The exception to that pattern is in Florida, where collections occurred after an extended period of high temperatures.

```{r}
#| label: continuous-temps
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
temp_profiles = temp_profiles %>% 
  filter(doy > 100) %>% 
  mutate(region = fct_relevel(region, "Florida", "Chesapeake", "Connecticut",
                              "Maine", "Shediac", "Miramichi"))

site_temps2 = site_temps %>% 
  mutate(region = case_when(
    site == "Manatee River" ~ "Florida",
    site == "Ft. Hamer" ~ "Florida",
    site == "Tyler Cove" ~ "Chesapeake",
    site == "Ganey's Wharf" ~ "Chesapeake",
    site == "Esker Point" ~ "Connecticut",
    site == "Sawyer Park" ~ "Maine",
    site == "St. Thomas de Kent Wharf" ~ "Shediac",
    site == "Ritchie Wharf" ~ "Miramichi"),
    region = fct_relevel(region, "Florida", "Chesapeake", "Connecticut",
                         "Maine", "Shediac", "Miramichi"))

ggplot(temp_profiles, aes(x = doy, y = temp_c)) + 
  facet_wrap(region~.) + 
  geom_point(data = site_temps2,
             aes(x = doy, y = collection_temp, colour = site),
             size = 3) +
  geom_line() + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_cols) + 
  labs(x = "Day of the Year", 
       y = "Mean Daily Temp. (°C)") + 
  theme_matt_facets() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none", 
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 320, hjust = 0, vjust = 0.5))
```

Exact locations for the sites are provided here:

```{r}
#| label: site-table
site_data %>%  
  arrange(lat) %>%  
  select("Site" = site, "Region" = region, "Lat" = lat, "Long" = long) %>% 
  knitr::kable(align = "c")
```

The latitudinal gradient covers a wide range of seasonality. Shown below is the temperature range. While based on collection temperatures, and therefore an underestimate of the total seasonal range of temperatures, these patterns are representative of the expected latitudinal gradient in seasonality.

```{r}
#| label: lat-temp-range-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
site_temps %>% 
  group_by(site, lat) %>%  
  summarise(temp_range = max(collection_temp) - min(collection_temp)) %>%  
  ggplot(aes(x = lat, y = temp_range)) + 
  geom_point(aes(colour = site),
             size = 3) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = site_cols) + 
  labs(x = "Latitude", 
       y = "Collection Temp. Range (°C)") + 
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

There was a general increase in the collection temperature range at warmer sites. This provides an opportunity to disentangle some of the traditionally proposed hypotheses about thermal adaptation (macrophysiological gradients often include stable and warm environments contrasted with cooler, more variable environment).

```{r}
#| label: max-temp-vs-range
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
site_temps %>% 
  group_by(site, lat) %>%  
  summarise(
    max_temp = max(collection_temp),
    temp_range = max(collection_temp) - min(collection_temp)) %>%  
  ggplot(aes(x = max_temp, y = temp_range)) + 
  geom_point(aes(colour = site),
             size = 3) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = site_cols) + 
  labs(x = "Max. Collection Temp. (°C)", 
       y = "Collection Temp. Range (°C)") + 
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

### Paired low- and high-salinity sites

Nested within each of the three regions (South, Central, and Northern regions) are pairs of low and high salinity sites:

```{r}
#| label: sal-table
data.frame("Region" = c("South", "Central", "North"),
           "Low Salinity" = c("Ft. Hamer", "Ganey's Wharf", "Ritchie Wharf"),
           "High Salinity" = c("Manatee River", "Tyler Cove", "St. Thomas de Kent Wharf")) %>% 
  knitr::kable(align = "c")
```

 

There are fairly well-established divergences between high salinity and low salinity populations of *Acartia tonsa*. These sets of geographically proximate sites potentially provide independent comparisons of the effects of seasonality across salinity gradients. Shown here are the collection conditions for these pairs of sites. Temperature was typically similar across the pairs within each collection, while salinity differences were fairly stable across collections.

```{r}
#| label: season-sal-comps
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8
season_cols = c("early" = "grey75", 
                "peak" = "grey50", 
                "late" = "grey25")

sal_regions = data.frame(region = rep(c("South", "Central", "North"), each = 2), 
                         site = c("Ft. Hamer", "Manatee River", 
                                  "Ganey's Wharf", "Tyler Cove", 
                                  "Ritchie Wharf", "St. Thomas de Kent Wharf"),
                         salinity = c("low", "high"))

sal_comps = join_data %>% 
  filter(site %in% sal_regions$site) %>% 
  inner_join(sal_regions, by = c("site")) %>% 
  select( region = region.y, site, salinity, season, doy, collection_temp, collection_salinity,
          size, ctmax, warming_tol) %>% 
  mutate(salinity = fct_relevel(salinity, "low", "high"),
         region = fct_relevel(region, "South", "Central", "North"))

sal_comp_temps = sal_comps %>%  
  select(salinity, season, region, collection_temp, collection_salinity) %>% 
  distinct() %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = salinity, y = collection_temp, colour = season, group = season)) + 
  facet_wrap(region~.) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) + 
  geom_point(size = 4) + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = season_cols) + 
  labs(y = "Collection Temp. (°C)",
       x = "") + 
  theme_matt_facets(base_size = 14)

sal_comp_sal = sal_comps %>%  
  select(salinity, season, region, collection_temp, collection_salinity) %>% 
  distinct() %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = salinity, y = collection_salinity, colour = season, group = season)) + 
  facet_wrap(region~.) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) + 
  geom_point(size = 4) + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = season_cols) + 
  labs(y = "Collection Salinity (psu)",
       x = "Salinity") + 
  theme_matt_facets(base_size = 14)

ggarrange(sal_comp_temps, sal_comp_sal, nrow = 2, common.legend = T, legend = "right")
```

### Generations between collections

```{r}

early_peak = join_data %>% 
  filter(season %in% c("early", "peak")) %>% 
  mutate(season = if_else(season == "early", "one", "two")) %>% 
  group_by(site) %>% 
  mutate(ctmax_sd_p = sd(ctmax),
         size_sd_p = sd(size), 
         temp_change = max(collection_temp) - min(collection_temp),
         avg_temp = (max(collection_temp) + min(collection_temp)) / 2,
         days_passed = max(doy) - min(doy)) %>% 
  select(site, lat, season, 
         ctmax_sd_p, size_sd_p, 
         temp_change, avg_temp, days_passed, 
         ctmax, size) %>%
  group_by(site, lat, season, 
           ctmax_sd_p, size_sd_p, 
           temp_change, avg_temp, days_passed) %>% 
  summarize(ctmax = mean(ctmax),
            size = mean(size)) %>% 
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(site, lat, ctmax_sd_p, size_sd_p, 
                          temp_change, avg_temp, days_passed), 
              names_from = season, 
              values_from = c(ctmax, size)) %>% 
  mutate(season = "early_to_peak") %>%  
  drop_na()

peak_late = join_data %>% 
  filter(season %in% c("peak", "late")) %>% 
  mutate(season = if_else(season == "peak", "one", "two")) %>% 
  group_by(site) %>% 
  mutate(ctmax_sd_p = sd(ctmax),
         size_sd_p = sd(size), 
         temp_change = last(collection_temp) - first(collection_temp),
         avg_temp = (max(collection_temp) + min(collection_temp)) / 2,
         days_passed = max(doy) - min(doy)) %>% 
  select(site, lat, season, ctmax_sd_p, size_sd_p, 
         temp_change, avg_temp, days_passed, 
         ctmax, size) %>%
  group_by(site, lat, season, ctmax_sd_p, size_sd_p, 
           temp_change, avg_temp, days_passed) %>% 
  summarize(ctmax = mean(ctmax),
            size = mean(size)) %>% 
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(site, lat, ctmax_sd_p, size_sd_p, 
                          temp_change, avg_temp, days_passed), 
              names_from = season, 
              values_from = c(ctmax, size)) %>% 
  mutate(season = "peak_to_late") %>%  
  drop_na()


generations = bind_rows(early_peak, peak_late) %>% 
  mutate("gen_time" = 5490*(avg_temp + 1)^-2.05,
         "gens" = floor(days_passed / gen_time))
```

```{r}
#| label: num-gens-plot
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
ggplot(generations, aes(x = lat, y = gens, colour = site, shape = season)) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1) + 
  geom_point(size = 5) + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_cols) + 
  labs(x = "Latitude", 
       y = "Generations between \ncollections") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(from = 0, to = 21, by = 5)) + 
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

## 2. Phenotypes: thermal limits and body size

### Critical Thermal Limits

A total of `r dim(all_data)[1]` individuals were examined. Critical thermal limits and body size measurements were made before individuals were preserved in ethanol. We excluded data for individuals that were either later classified as males or juveniles, that we were unable to assign to a clade, or that were identified as individuals from a closely related species (*Acartia hudsonica*). With these individuals excluded, the full data set contains `r dim(join_data)[1]` adult females with CTmax and body size measurements, and clade identifications.

Critical thermal maxima (CTmax) was measured using a custom setup. The method uses a standard dynamic ramping assay to determine the maximum temperature individuals could sustain normal functioning. This differs from lethal temperatures, and indeed, all individuals recovered following the assay.

Individuals were rested for one hour after collection before the assay. During the assay, copepods were held in artificial seawater, composed of bottled spring water and Instant Ocean salt mix adjusted to match collection salinities. During the assay, several 'control' individuals were maintained in this solution at ambient temperatures without the temperature ramp to ensure that there was no background changes in behavior or mortality. When sorting individuals from the plankton tow contents, they were held in a 50:50 mix of 60 um filtered water from the collection site and artificial seawater as an additional acclimation step.

Sample sizes varied slightly across experiments, but generally \~20 individuals were measured per season at each site. The major exceptions were the early samples from the Florida sites and the late sample from Sawyer Park (Maine). Only two sets of samples (peak and late) were collected from Fort Hamer and Manatee River. The late season collection from Sawyer Park occurred after *Acartia tonsa* abundance decreased, and samples were dominated by *Acartia hudsonica*. Thermal limits were measured for all *A. tonsa* individuals recovered. No samples were collected from Key Largo for this project, as *Acartia tonsa* wasn't present in the water during the peak season, likely due to a recent extreme heat event.

```{r}
join_data %>%  
  group_by(site, season) %>% 
  count() %>%  
  pivot_wider(id_cols = "site", 
              names_from = season, 
              values_from = n, 
              values_fill = 0) %>% 
  select(site, early, peak, late) %>% 
  knitr::kable()
```

Shown below are the measured CTmax values. Individual measurements are shown in small points for each collection. The large points indicate the mean values for each collection.

```{r}
#| label: seasonal-ct-max
mean_ctmax = join_data %>% 
  filter(clade!="A_hudsonica") %>% 
  group_by(site, season, doy, collection_temp) %>% 
  summarize(mean_ctmax = mean(ctmax),
            median_ctmax = median(ctmax))

ctmax_plot = join_data %>% 
  filter(clade!="A_hudsonica") %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = season, y = ctmax, colour = site)) + 
  geom_line(data = mean_ctmax, 
            aes(y = mean_ctmax, group = site),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.4),
            linewidth = 1) + 
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.1, jitter.height = 0,
                                             dodge.width = 0.4),
             alpha = 0.3) + 
  geom_point(data = mean_ctmax, 
             aes(y = mean_ctmax),
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.4),
             size = 4) + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_cols) + 
  labs(y = "CTmax (°C)",
       x = "Season") +
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "right", 
        legend.title.align = 0.125)
```

### Body Size

Following the CTmax assay, individuals were photographed for body size measurements. Prosome lengths were measured from these photographs using a scale micrometer and the software ImageJ. These measurements are shown below. As before, large points indicate the mean body size. While less cohesive than CTmax, a general trend of increasing body size with latitude and time of year can be seen.

```{r}
#| label: seasonal-body-size
mean_size = join_data %>% 
  filter(clade != "A_hudsonica") %>% 
  group_by(site, season, doy, collection_temp) %>% 
  summarize(mean_size = mean(size),
            median_size = median(size))

size_plot = join_data %>% 
  filter(clade != "A_hudsonica") %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = season, y = size, colour = site)) + 
  geom_line(data = mean_size, 
            aes(y = mean_size, group = site),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.4),
            linewidth = 1) + 
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.1, jitter.height = 0,
                                             dodge.width = 0.4),
             alpha = 0.3) + 
  geom_point(data = mean_size, 
             aes(y = mean_size),
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.4),
             size = 4) + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_cols) + 
  labs(y = "Prosome Length (mm)",
       x = "Season") +
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "right", 
        legend.title.align = 0.125)
```

### Warming tolerance

Warming tolerance (the difference between thermal limits and environmental temperatures) is a commonly used metric of climate vulnerability. We calculated this as the difference between measured CTmax values and the collection temperature. Smaller warming tolerance values indicate that populations were nearer to their upper thermal limits, suggesting greater vulnerability.

```{r}
#| label: seasonal-warming-tol
mean_wt = join_data %>% 
  filter(clade!="A_hudsonica") %>% 
  group_by(site, season) %>% 
  summarize(mean_wt = mean(warming_tol),
            median_wt = median(warming_tol))

ggplot(join_data, aes(x = season, y = warming_tol, colour = site)) + 
  geom_line(data = mean_wt, 
            aes(y = mean_wt, group = site),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.4),
            linewidth = 1) + 
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.1, jitter.height = 0,
                                             dodge.width = 0.4),
             alpha = 0.3) + 
  geom_point(data = mean_wt, 
             aes(y = mean_wt),
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.4),
             size = 4) + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_cols) + 
  labs(y = "Warming Tolerance (°C)",
       x = "Season") +
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "right", 
        legend.title.align = 0.125)
```

### Trait correlations

Regardless of the underlying mechanism (genetic differentiation or phenotypic plasticity), we expect that collections from warmer waters should yield copepods with higher thermal limits and smaller body sizes. Our observations largely fit this expectation, with strong increases in CTmax at higher temperatures, and a general decrease in prosome lengths as temperature increased. There was a larger correlation between CTmax and temperature than size and temperature. There are myriad reasons this might be observed, but one potential is the potential for acclimation of thermal limits. Body size is fixed in the adult stage, while CTmax can continue to vary as water temperature changes. This is indirect evidence for the importance of rapid acclimation in the observed patterns.

The relationship between prosome length and CTmax is also of interest. Given that larger body sizes are associated with cold adaptation/acclimation, it is unsurprising that there is a general trend of decreasing thermal limits with increasing size. Individual regression lines for each site are also included - the dark grey lines in the background represent the 'universal' regression for that site, with individual colored regression lines for each collection. At most sites, evidence for this negative relationship between CTmax and body size is observed across collections rather than within collections, suggesting this relationship is primaly a reflection of the response to seasonal temperature variation.

### Paired sites: trait differences

The three pairs of cross-salinity comparisons do show evidence for fine-scale trait divergence, although there was no consistent pattern in the direction or magnitude of differences. CTmax was similar across sites in the Southern and Central pairs. In the Northern pair, CTmax tended to be slightly lower for individuals from the low salinity site. Size was more variable between the paired sites. In the South, individuals from the low salinity site were consistently smaller than individuals from the high salinity site, despite experiencing similar temperatures. By contrast, in the Central pair individuals from the low salinity site tended to be slightly larger than those from the high salinity site, although the magnitude of this difference this varied seasonally. In the Northern pair, individuals from the low salinity site were slightly larger than individuals from the high salinity site during the early and peak season collections, but there was an abrupt reversal of this pattern during the late collection, when individuals from the high salinity site were much larger than individuals from the low salinity site.

Note that two of the three pairs also differ in clade composition: Manatee River and Ft. Hamer hold different F lineages (F-MR, F-FH), and St. Thomas de Kent Wharf and Ritchie Wharf differ in their mix of clades X and IV (Section 3). Differences between paired sites therefore combine environment, lineage and clade composition; Section 4 separates them.

## 3. Low-coverage whole genome data

After phenotyping, each individual was preserved in 95% ethanol. Individual DNA libraries were prepared using Twist Bio 96-plex prep kits, then sequenced on two lanes of an Illumina NovaSeq X Plus 25B by Novogene (436 libraries). Read processing, mapping, site filtering, clade assignment and population genomic analyses were run on the Unity cluster (Snakemake project `aton_lcwg`). The figures in this section are built from the exported result tables (`Raw_data/cluster_exports/`; export in use: `r export_name`). *Acartia hudsonica* libraries are excluded throughout.

```{r}
#| label: cluster-tables
#| include: false
read_cx <- function(...) {
  f <- cx(...)
  if (file.exists(f)) read_tsv(f, show_col_types = FALSE, comment = "#") else NULL
}
fastp   <- read_cx("results", "00_qc", "fastp_summary.tsv")
depth_c <- read_cx("results", "02_sites", "depth_by_clade", "depth_by_clade.tsv")
unmask  <- read_cx("results", "02_sites", "sites", "unmasked_nuclear_summary.tsv")
final_s <- read_cx("results", "02_sites", "sites", "final_sites_summary.tsv")
paralog <- read_cx("results", "02_sites", "masks", "ngsparalog_summary.tsv")
mito    <- read_cx("results", "03_clades", "mito", "mito_read_split.tsv")
clades  <- read_cx("metadata", "clade_assignments.tsv")

seq_plot <- seq_data %>%
  left_join(select(fastp, sample_id, gc_after), by = "sample_id") %>%
  mutate(status = if_else(library_failed, "failed library", as.character(clade)),
         status = factor(status, levels = c(tonsa_clades, "failed library")),
         depth_per_10M = mean_depth_nuclear / (raw_reads / 1e7))

status_cols <- c(clade_cols[tonsa_clades], "failed library" = "grey75")
```

### Sequencing summary

Reads per library varied over two orders of magnitude; 23 libraries failed (\< 500,000 reads, 20 of them on plate 5). The reference genome is closest to clade X: the other clades map less well and yield less usable depth per read, on every plate. Libraries with low mapping and high GC content carry DNA from other organisms (Section 3.3).

```{r}

  geom_boxplot(data = ~ filter(.x, !library_failed), outlier.shape = NA, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = status), width = 0.15, height = 0, size = 1.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = status_cols) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Plate", y = "Reads (millions, log scale)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_matt(base_size = 14)

p_map <- seq_plot %>% filter(!library_failed, clade %in% tonsa_clades) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(clade, levels = tonsa_clades), y = pct_mapped, fill = clade)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = clade_cols, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Clade", y = "% reads mapped") +

p_bias <- seq_plot %>% filter(!library_failed, clade %in% tonsa_clades) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(clade, levels = tonsa_clades), y = depth_per_10M, fill = clade)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = clade_cols, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Clade", y = "Nuclear depth per 10 M reads") +

  mutate(clade = factor(clade, levels = tonsa_clades)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = 100 * gc_after, y = pct_mapped, colour = clade, shape = clade)) +
```

### Site filtering

Genotype-likelihood analyses use only the 15 chromosomes, minus soft-masked repeats, nuclear copies of mitochondrial DNA (NUMTs) and SNPs flagged as collapsed paralogs by ngsParalog. Because of the reference bias, far fewer sites pass the missing-data filter (data in at least 50% of individuals) in clades S and IV than in X.

```{r}
#| label: site-filtering
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5
genome_mb <- 779.75
cascade <- tibble(
  step = c("Assembly", "15 chromosomes", "Repeats removed", "Final sites"),
  mb = c(genome_mb, sum(unmask$length) / 1e6, sum(unmask$unmasked_bp) / 1e6,
         sum(final_s$unmasked_bp) / 1e6)) %>%
  mutate(step = factor(step, levels = step))

p_cascade <- ggplot(cascade, aes(x = step, y = mb)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey60", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f", mb)), vjust = -0.4, size = 4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Megabases") +
  theme_matt(base_size = 13) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))

p_access <- depth_c %>%
  filter(clade %in% tonsa_clades) %>%
  mutate(clade = factor(clade, levels = tonsa_clades)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = clade, y = sites_counted / 1e6, fill = clade)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = clade_cols, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Clade", y = "Mb with data in ≥ 50%\nof individuals") +
  theme_matt(base_size = 13)

p_paralog <- paralog %>%
  filter(clade %in% tonsa_clades) %>%
  mutate(clade = factor(clade, levels = tonsa_clades)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = clade, y = pct_flagged, fill = clade)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = clade_cols, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Clade", y = "% candidate SNPs flagged\nas paralogs") +
  theme_matt(base_size = 13)

ggarrange(p_cascade, p_access, p_paralog, nrow = 1, labels = "AUTO", widths = c(1.3, 1, 1))
```

### Clade identity

Clades were assigned in two independent ways. **Mitochondrial:** each individual's reads were mapped to one partial mitogenome per clade, and the clade was taken from the reads covering the COI barcode region. **Nuclear:** genome-wide genotype likelihoods (PCAngsd, NGSadmix) on all kept libraries. The two agree for every individual. Two libraries contained DNA from individuals of two different clades (both mitochondrial and nuclear signals mixed) and were excluded.

```{r}
#| label: mito-read-split
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 9
mito_long <- mito %>%
  select(sample_id, starts_with("coi_reads_mtDNA_")) %>%
  pivot_longer(-sample_id, names_to = "contig", values_to = "reads",
               names_prefix = "coi_reads_mtDNA_") %>%
  group_by(sample_id) %>%
  mutate(prop = reads / sum(reads)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  inner_join(select(seq_data, sample_id, site_code, season, replicate, tube), by = "sample_id") %>%
  mutate(contig = factor(contig, levels = tonsa_clades),
         ind = sprintf("%d_%02d", replicate, tube))

ggplot(mito_long, aes(x = ind, y = prop, fill = contig)) +
  facet_grid(site_code ~ season) +
  geom_col(width = 1, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = clade_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Individual (assay_tube)", y = "Share of COI reads", fill = "Mito contig") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 290, hjust = 0, vjust = 0.5, size = 7))
```

All four clades are cleanly separated in the nuclear genome. Clade F splits further into site-specific sub-lineages (Manatee River, Ft. Hamer, and the Chesapeake/New England group), visible on PC4 and at K = 5–6.

```{r}
#| label: clade-structure
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 10
pca_full <- read_cx("results", "04_structure", "all", "pcangsd_scores.tsv")
cov_all <- as.matrix(read.table(cx("results", "04_structure", "all", "pcangsd.cov")))
ve <- eigen(cov_all, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
ve <- round(100 * ve / sum(ve), 1)

# PCAngsd / NGSadmix were run on all kept libraries; the two mixed (unassigned)
# libraries are dropped from the plots only
pca_full <- pca_full %>%
  left_join(select(clades, sample_id, clade, lineage), by = "sample_id")
pca_all <- pca_full %>%
  filter(clade %in% tonsa_clades) %>%
  mutate(clade = factor(clade, levels = tonsa_clades))

pca_plot <- function(a, b) {
  ggplot(pca_all, aes(x = .data[[a]], y = .data[[b]], colour = clade, shape = clade)) +
    geom_point(size = 2.2, alpha = 0.85) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = clade_cols[tonsa_clades]) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = clade_shapes[tonsa_clades]) +
    labs(x = sprintf("%s (%.1f%%)", a, ve[as.integer(sub("PC", "", a))]),
         y = sprintf("%s (%.1f%%)", b, ve[as.integer(sub("PC", "", b))]),
         colour = "Clade", shape = "Clade") +
    theme_matt(base_size = 13)
}

# NGSadmix: best of 3 runs per K; clusters coloured by the clade that dominates them
best_run <- function(K) {
  likes <- sapply(1:3, function(r) {
    l <- readLines(cx("results", "04_structure", "all", "ngsadmix", sprintf("K%d_rep%d.log", K, r)))
    as.numeric(sub(".*best like=([-0-9.e]+).*", "\\1", grep("best like", l, value = TRUE)[1]))
  })
  which.max(likes)
}
ord <- pca_all %>%
  mutate(lin = factor(lineage, levels = c("X", "S", "IV", "F-N", "F-NE", "F-FH", "F-MR")),
         site_code = factor(site, levels = site_order)) %>%
  arrange(lin, site_code, sampling_event) %>% pull(sample_id)
f_shades <- c(clade_cols[["F"]], "#F36E6D", "#7C2B2B", "#FFB3B2")   # F plus lighter / darker shades
admix <- map_dfr(3:6, function(K) {
  q <- read.table(cx("results", "04_structure", "all", "ngsadmix", sprintf("K%d_rep%d.qopt", K, best_run(K))))
  q$sample_id <- pca_full$sample_id   # rows follow the full analysis set
  long <- pivot_longer(q, -sample_id, names_to = "cluster", values_to = "q") %>%
    filter(sample_id %in% pca_all$sample_id)
  dom <- long %>% group_by(sample_id) %>% slice_max(q, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>% ungroup() %>%
    left_join(select(pca_all, sample_id, clade), by = "sample_id") %>%
    count(cluster, clade) %>% group_by(cluster) %>% slice_max(n, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
  long %>% left_join(select(dom, cluster, top = clade), by = "cluster") %>% mutate(K = paste0("K = ", K))
}) %>%
  mutate(sample_id = factor(sample_id, levels = ord))
fill_map <- admix %>% distinct(K, cluster, top) %>% group_by(K, top) %>%
  mutate(col = if_else(top == "F", f_shades[row_number()], clade_cols[as.character(top)])) %>%
  ungroup() %>% mutate(key = paste(K, cluster))
admix <- admix %>% mutate(key = paste(K, cluster))

p_admix <- ggplot(admix, aes(x = sample_id, y = q, fill = key)) +
  facet_grid(K ~ .) +
  geom_col(width = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(fill_map$col, fill_map$key), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Individuals, grouped by lineage (X, S, IV, F-N, F-NE, F-FH, F-MR) and site", y = "Ancestry") +
  theme_matt_facets(base_size = 13) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())

ggarrange(ggarrange(pca_plot("PC1", "PC2"), pca_plot("PC3", "PC4"), nrow = 1,
                    common.legend = TRUE, legend = "right", labels = c("A", "B")),
          p_admix, nrow = 2, heights = c(1, 1.1), labels = c("", "C"))
```

Within clade F, the sub-lineages are clearly separated (2–6% COI divergence) but much less divergent than the clades are from each other (12–18%). We therefore analyse four clades, and keep the F sub-lineage as an annotation.

```{r}
#| label: coi-divergence
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
fa <- readLines(cx("results", "03_clades", "mito", "coi_aligned.fa"))
hdr <- grepl("^>", fa)
seq_id <- sub("^>(\\S+).*", "\\1", fa[hdr])
seqs <- tapply(fa[!hdr], cumsum(hdr)[!hdr], paste, collapse = "")
names(seqs) <- seq_id
lin <- clades %>% filter(clade %in% tonsa_clades, sample_id %in% seq_id) %>%
  mutate(group = if_else(clade == "F", lineage, clade))
mat <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(toupper(seqs[lin$sample_id]), ""))
ok <- matrix(mat %in% c("A", "C", "G", "T"), nrow = nrow(mat))
n <- nrow(mat); diff <- matrix(0, n, n); comp <- matrix(0, n, n)
for (j in seq_len(ncol(mat))) {
  v <- ok[, j]
  both <- outer(v, v, "&")
  comp <- comp + both
  diff <- diff + (outer(mat[, j], mat[, j], "!=") & both)
}
pd <- diff / comp
grp <- lin$group
grp_levels <- intersect(c("X", "S", "IV", "F-N", "F-NE", "F-FH", "F-MR"), unique(grp))
div <- expand_grid(a = grp_levels, b = grp_levels) %>%
  mutate(pdist = map2_dbl(a, b, function(x, y) {
    m <- pd[grp == x, grp == y, drop = FALSE]
    if (x == y) mean(m[upper.tri(m)]) else mean(m)
  }) * 100,
  a = factor(a, levels = grp_levels), b = factor(b, levels = rev(grp_levels)))

ggplot(div, aes(x = a, y = b, fill = pdist)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", pdist), colour = pdist > 9), size = 4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "white", "FALSE" = "grey15"), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F2F2F0", high = "#2B2B29", name = "COI\ndistance (%)") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_matt(base_size = 13) +
  theme(axis.line = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank())
```

### Genetic differentiation within clades

Population structure and diversity are analysed within each clade (X, F, S, IV), with populations defined as clade × site × sampling event (n ≥ 8). Within clade F, site differences include differences between F sub-lineages.

```{r}
#| label: within-clade-pca
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 9
wpca <- map_dfr(tonsa_clades, function(cl) {
  f <- cx("results", "04_structure", cl, "pcangsd_scores.tsv")
  if (!file.exists(f)) return(NULL)
  cv <- as.matrix(read.table(cx("results", "04_structure", cl, "pcangsd.cov")))
  v <- eigen(cv, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
  read_tsv(f, show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
    transmute(sample_id, PC1, PC2, site, season = sampling_event,
              panel = sprintf("%s (n = %d): PC1 %.1f%%, PC2 %.1f%%", cl, n(), 100 * v[1] / sum(v), 100 * v[2] / sum(v)))
})
if (nrow(wpca) == 0) {
  cat("Within-clade PCAs are not in this export yet.")
} else {
  wpca %>%
    mutate(site = factor(site, levels = site_order),
           season = factor(season, levels = season_order),
           panel = factor(panel, levels = unique(panel))) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, fill = site, shape = season)) +
    facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free") +
    geom_point(size = 5, colour = "grey15", stroke = 0.3) +
    # 95% ellipse per site (t distribution, so a few outlying individuals don't
    # inflate it); sites with fewer than 4 individuals in a clade get no ellipse
    # stat_ellipse(data = ~ add_count(.x, panel, site) %>% filter(n >= 4),
    #              aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = site, group = site), inherit.aes = FALSE,
    #              type = "t", level = 0.95, linewidth = 1.5) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = pop_cols[site_order], guide = "none") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = pop_cols[site_order], drop = FALSE) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(early = 21, peak = 24, late = 22)) +
    guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(shape = 21))) +
    labs(fill = "Site", shape = "Season") +
    theme_matt_facets(base_size = 13)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fst-pairs
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
fst_files <- Sys.glob(cx("results", "05_diversity", "fst", "*.fst.global.txt"))
if (length(fst_files) == 0) {
  cat("FST results are not in this export yet.")
} else {
  fst <- map_dfr(fst_files, function(f) {
    vals <- as.numeric(regmatches(readLines(f, warn = FALSE), gregexpr("-?[0-9.]+(e-?[0-9]+)?", readLines(f, warn = FALSE)))[[1]])
    pops <- strsplit(sub("\\.fst\\.global\\.txt$", "", basename(f)), ".vs.", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
    tibble(pop1 = pops[1], pop2 = pops[2], fst_unweighted = tail(vals, 2)[1], fst_weighted = tail(vals, 1))
  }) %>%
    separate(pop1, c("clade", "site1", "season1"), sep = "__") %>%
    separate(pop2, c("clade2", "site2", "season2"), sep = "__") %>%
    filter(clade %in% tonsa_clades) %>%
    mutate(comparison = case_when(site1 == site2 ~ "seasonal (same site)",
                                  season1 == season2 ~ "spatial (same season)",
                                  TRUE ~ "site and season differ"),
           clade = factor(clade, levels = tonsa_clades))
  write_csv(fst, here("Output", "Output_data", "fst_pairs.csv"))
  
  ggplot(fst, aes(x = comparison, y = fst_weighted, fill = clade)) +
    geom_boxplot(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) + 
    geom_point(size = 2.5, position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = clade_cols) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = expression(F[ST]~"(weighted)")) +
    theme_matt_facets(base_size = 13) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
}
```

Shown below are estimates of diversity across the data set. Tajima's D can be used to detect random vs. non-random evolutionary processes (e.g. drift vs. selection). A value near zero indicates neutral processes and a stable population size. Negative values indicate an excess of rare alleles, suggesting possible recent selective sweeps or population expansion after a bottleneck. Positive values indicate possible population contraction or balancing selection, resulting in fewer rare alleles than expected.

Most values of Tajima's D for our data set are small (within 0.5 of 0). A few samples reached moderate values around -1 and 1. Interestingly, all cases are from the two sites in the Chesapeake, with a low Tajima's D value for S clade individuals at the high salinity site, and high values for F clade individuals at both high and low salinity sites.

We also calculated nucleotide diversity, which represents the average number of nucleotide differences between randomly sampled sequences in a population. Theta values tended to be high, with the exception of F Clade individuals at the low salinity site in Florida and the two sites in the Chesapeake.

We note that these diversity metrics should only be compared within clades since reference bias changes which sites are usable in each clade.

Within sites, there is notably little change in these metrics across seasons. Three general within-clade patterns can be seen across sites:

1.  **Increasing Tajima's D and decreased nucleotide diversity,** as seen in Clade F. This may indicate serial founder effects. Diversity should fall steadily in the direction of expansion ([Excoffier et al. 2009](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.ecolsys.39.110707.173414)). For a clade spreading north since the last glacial maximum, northern sites would be expected to have lower θπ and higher D ([Hewitt 2000](https://doi.org/10.1038/35016000)). This suggests a low latitude origin for this clade.
2.  **Consistently low Tajima's D and consistently high nucleotide diversity**, as seen in Clades S and IV (although note the limited sampling for these clades). This pattern suggests large, well-connected populations. There may have been population expansion before sites diverged, or there may be substantial gene flow between populations keeping them similar ([Excoffier et al. 2009](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.ecolsys.39.110707.173414)).
3.  **Consistently small Tajima's D and consistently high nucleotide diversity**, as seen in Clade X. While this typically would indicate large, stable populations, Clade X is found only at the high latitude sites, where populations of *Acartia tonsa* are present during only part of the year, exhibiting drastic fluctuations in population size over this period. This may indicate the importance of an egg bank / resting eggs. If the population is generated each year by hatching out of eggs laid over many previous years, diversity would remain high. The egg bank acts as a store of diversity, so a brief active season doesn’t mean a small genetic population ([Hairston 1996](https://doi.org/10.4319/lo.1996.41.5.1087)). Resting eggs are well documented in *Acartia* (Marcus 1996, *Hydrobiologia* 320:141–152). In Narragansett Bay, *A. tonsa* replaces the egg-banking *A. hudsonica* each summer ([Sullivan & McManus 1986](https://doi.org/10.3354/meps028121)), the same seasonal turnover your ME site shows. Under these dynamics, individual sites may retain distinct populations, as seen in the within-clade PCAs above.

```{r}
#| label: diversity-pops
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
theta_files <- Sys.glob(cx("results", "05_diversity", "thetas", "*.genome.tsv"))
if (length(theta_files) == 0) {
  cat("Diversity estimates are not in this export yet.")
} else {
  tajima <- function(pop) {
    f <- cx("results", "05_diversity", "thetas", paste0(pop, ".thetas.idx.pestPG"))
    if (!file.exists(f)) return(NA_real_)
    t <- read.table(f, comment.char = "", skip = 1)
    weighted.mean(t[[9]], t[[14]])    # Tajima's D per chromosome, weighted by sites
  }
  div_pop <- map_dfr(theta_files, ~ read_tsv(.x, show_col_types = FALSE)) %>%
    mutate(tajima_D = map_dbl(population, tajima)) %>%
    separate(population, c("clade", "site", "season"), sep = "__", remove = FALSE) %>%
    filter(clade %in% tonsa_clades) %>%
    mutate(clade = factor(clade, levels = tonsa_clades),
           site = factor(site, levels = site_order),
           season = factor(season, levels = season_order))
  write_csv(div_pop, here("Output", "Output_data", "diversity_populations.csv"))
  div_pop %>%
    select(clade, site, season, `θπ per site` = pi_per_site, `Tajima's D` = tajima_D) %>%
    pivot_longer(c(`θπ per site`, `Tajima's D`), names_to = "stat") %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = site, y = value, shape = season, colour = clade)) +
    facet_grid(stat ~ ., scales = "free", space = "free_x") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey") + 
    geom_point(size = 5) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = clade_cols) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(early = 16, peak = 17, late = 15)) +
    labs(x = "Site (south → north)", y = NULL, shape = "Season") +
    theme_matt_facets(base_size = 13)
}
```

### Parasites and symbionts

Reads that did not map to the *A. tonsa* reference were screened for small-subunit rRNA (phyloFlash, SILVA 138.1). Each read pair was assigned to the shared ancestor of all equally good database hits, at a rank limited by its identity, and host (*Acartia*) rRNA was removed. An organism group was called present at ≥ 5 read pairs and ≥ 2 per million library pairs (`Scripts/04_micro_calls.R`). Parasites (*Paradinium*, trematodes) and epibionts (apostome and peritrich ciliates) show strong site × season patterns: apostomes in every Connecticut late-season individual, trematodes in most Ritchie Wharf peak-season individuals, and *Zoothamnium* on late-season Maine and St. Thomas de Kent Wharf copepods.

```{r}
#| label: micro-setup
#| include: false
micro_groups <- read_csv(od("micro_groups.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
micro_labels <- c(paradinium = "Paradinium (parasite)", trematode = "Hemiuroid trematodes",
                  apostome = "Apostome ciliates", peritrich = "Peritrich ciliates (Zoothamnium)",
                  cnidaria_myxozoa = "Cnidaria / Myxozoa", kinetoplastid = "Kinetoplastids (background)",
                  malacostraca = "Malacostraca (diet)")
micro_ind <- seq_data %>%
  filter(clade %in% tonsa_clades, !library_failed) %>%
  select(sample_id, site_code, season, clade, ends_with("_call"), ends_with("_per_M")) %>%
  pivot_longer(-c(sample_id, site_code, season, clade),
               names_to = c("group", ".value"), names_pattern = "(.*)_(call|per_M)") %>%
  filter(group %in% names(micro_labels))

micro_prev <- function(groups) {
  micro_ind %>%
    filter(group %in% groups) %>%
    group_by(group, site_code, season) %>%
    summarise(n = n(), k = sum(call), .groups = "drop") %>%
    complete(group = groups, site_code = factor(site_order, levels = levels(site_code)),
             season = factor(season_order, levels = season_order)) %>%
    mutate(prev = k / n,
           group = factor(micro_labels[group], levels = rev(micro_labels[groups])),
           site_code = factor(site_code, levels = site_order))
}

prev_plot <- function(d) {
  ggplot(d, aes(x = site_code, y = group)) +
    facet_grid(~ season) +
    geom_text(data = ~ filter(.x, is.na(n)), label = "–", size = 4, colour = "grey60") +
    geom_point(data = ~ filter(.x, !is.na(n), k == 0), shape = 1, size = 1.5, colour = "grey75") +
    geom_point(data = ~ filter(.x, k > 0), aes(size = prev), colour = "grey15") +
    geom_text(data = ~ filter(.x, k > 0), aes(label = paste0(k, "/", n)),
              nudge_y = -0.35, size = 3, colour = "grey45") +
    scale_size_area(max_size = 12, breaks = c(0.1, 0.3, 0.6, 1), labels = scales::percent,
                    name = "Individuals\npositive") +
    labs(x = "Site (south → north)", y = NULL) +
    theme_matt_facets(base_size = 13) +
    theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "grey92"))
}

strip_plot <- function(groups) {
  d <- micro_ind %>%
    filter(group %in% groups) %>%
    arrange(site_code, season, clade) %>%
    mutate(sample_id = factor(sample_id, levels = unique(sample_id)),
           group = factor(micro_labels[group], levels = rev(micro_labels[groups])),
           per_M = na_if(per_M, 0))
  bar <- distinct(d, sample_id, clade, site_code, season) %>%
    mutate(clade = factor(clade, levels = tonsa_clades))
  p_bar <- ggplot(bar, aes(x = sample_id, y = 1, fill = clade)) +
    facet_grid(~ site_code + season, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") +
    geom_tile() +
    scale_fill_manual(values = clade_cols) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Clade") +
    theme_void(base_size = 11) +
    theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 8), legend.position = "right",
          panel.spacing = unit(2, "pt"))
  p_heat <- ggplot(d, aes(x = sample_id, y = group, fill = per_M)) +
    facet_grid(~ site_code + season, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") +
    geom_tile() +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "#E4E4E0", high = "#111110", trans = "log10", na.value = "white",
                        name = "Pairs per\nmillion") +
    labs(x = "Individuals, grouped by site and season", y = NULL) +
    theme_matt_facets(base_size = 11) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
          strip.text = element_blank(), strip.background = element_blank(),
          panel.spacing = unit(2, "pt"))
  ggarrange(p_bar, p_heat, ncol = 1, heights = c(0.25, 1), align = "v")
}

main_groups <- c("paradinium", "trematode", "apostome", "peritrich", "cnidaria_myxozoa")
all_groups  <- names(micro_labels)
```

```{r}

#| fig-width: 13
```


## 4. Clade-specific physiological patterns

### CTmax model

To more formally test the relationships between CTmax, collection temperature, and size, we used a linear mixed effects model, structured as `ctmax ~ clade * temp_cent + size + (1 + temp_cent|site) + (1|tube)`. This examines the effects of clade, temperature and size on CTmax, along with clade-specific effects of temperature. Collection temperature was centered before model fitting. The model also includes random intercepts for each site and the tube number (the position of each individual within the water bath during the CTmax assay).

```{r}
#| label: ctmax-model
#| include: false
filtered_data = join_data %>% 
  filter(clade != "A_hudsonica") %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  drop_na(size, ctmax) %>% 
  mutate(ctmax_cent = scale(ctmax, scale = F)[,1],
         temp_cent = scale(collection_temp, scale = F)[,1],
         size_cent = scale(size, scale = F)[,1],
         sal_cent = scale(collection_salinity, scale = F)[,1],
         sal_type = if_else(collection_salinity > 15, "High", "Low"), 
         replicate = factor(replicate))

ctmax.model = lme4::lmer(data = filtered_data, 
                         ctmax ~ clade * temp_cent + size + (1 | site) + (1 | replicate) + (1|tube))

performance::check_model(ctmax.model)

lmerTest::ranova(ctmax.model)
car::Anova(ctmax.model, type = "III")

```

The Stage 1 clade calls (Section 3.1) were merged with the CTmax and body size data set to examine clade-specific patterns of divergence. By plotting CTmax and size against the collection temperature we can see that these clades appear to be physiologically differentiated. Clades F and S tend to have higher CTmax, even when collected at the same temperatures as Clades X and IV. Size is more variable, with varying degrees of temperature sensitivity across the clades. Overall, however, Clade F tends to be smaller than Clades S and X. Clade IV tended to be the largest.

The general result here is that Clade F appears to be more thermally tolerant than Clades S and X, which in turn are more thermally tolerant than Clade IV. Clade IV does however, appear to exibit stronger plasticity than the other clades (although this pattern is only marginally significant in two of the comparisons; IV-S and IV-X)

These differences in physiology correspond to the distributional patterns for each clade. Using a Loess smoother (span = 2) highlights how the proportional abundance of the clades is affected by temperature in different ways. Clade F occurs in high proportion at high temperature, Clade IV occurs in high proportions at low temperatures, while Clade X occurs in high proportions at intermediate temperatures. Clade S generally occurs in low proportions, with a few exceptions.


### Trait variability within clades

Shown below is the trait variation (ranges) for each site. Ranges are calculated for each collection separately.

```{r}
#| label: trait-range-plot
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5
trait_ranges = join_data %>% 
  drop_na(clade) %>% 
  filter(clade != "A_hudsonica") %>% 
  group_by(site, season, clade, collection_temp, collection_salinity, doy, lat) %>% 
  summarise(mean_ctmax = mean(ctmax),
            ctmax_range = max(ctmax) - min(ctmax),
            ctmax_var = var(ctmax),
            mean_size = mean(size),
            size_range = max(size) - min(size),
            size_var = var(size)) %>% 
  mutate(prop_ctmax_range = ctmax_range / mean_ctmax,
         prop_size_range = size_range / mean_size)

ctmax_range_temp = ggplot(trait_ranges, aes(x = collection_temp, y = ctmax_range)) + 
  facet_wrap(clade~.) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "black", se = F) + 
  geom_point(aes(colour = site), 
             size = 3) + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_cols) + 
  labs(y = "CTmax Range (°C)",
       x = "Collection Temp. (°C)") +
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "right")

ctmax_var_temp = ggplot(trait_ranges, aes(x = collection_temp, y = ctmax_var, colour = site)) + 
  facet_wrap(clade~.) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "black", se = F) + 
  geom_point(aes(colour = site), 
             size = 3) + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_cols) + 
  labs(y = "CTmax Variance",
       x = "Collection Temp. (°C)") +
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "right")

size_range_temp = ggplot(trait_ranges, aes(x = collection_temp, y = size_range, colour = site)) + 
  facet_wrap(clade~.) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "black", se = F) + 
  geom_point(aes(colour = site), 
             size = 3) + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_cols) + 
  labs(y = "Size Range (mm)",
       x = "Collection Temp. (°C)") +
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "right")

size_var_temp = ggplot(trait_ranges, aes(x = collection_temp, y = size_var, colour = site)) + 
  facet_wrap(clade~.) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "black", se = F) + 
  geom_point(aes(colour = site), 
             size = 3) + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_cols) + 
  labs(y = "Size Variance",
       x = "Collection Temp. (°C)") +
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "right")

ggarrange(ctmax_var_temp, size_var_temp, common.legend = T, legend = "right")
```

Changes in trait variance may be indicative of phenotypic selection. If selection (as opposed to acclimation) are driving seasonal changes, we may expect to see a reduction in variance in the peak samples relative to the early season samples. Note that early season collection temperatures this year were higher than expected, driven by fairly strong heatwaves across the North Atlantic. As shown in the temperature profiles for each site, the 'early' samples were collected just after high temperatures were reached, while 'peak' samples were collected after sites had experienced high temperatures for several weeks (generations). As warming tolerances were fairly high throughout this period, we will assume that selection was weak before the early samples. If the early onset of high temperatures filtered out vulnerable genotypes prior to our sampling, the results will be a conservative estimate of the effects of selection on trait variance.

### Parasites, epibionts and thermal limits

Infected and uninfected individuals are compared within the same collection (same site, date and collection temperature), so differences are not confounded with acclimation temperature. Only collections with at least two positive and two negative individuals are shown.

```{r}
#| label: infection-traits
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7
inf_groups <- c(paradinium = "Paradinium", trematode = "Trematodes",
                apostome = "Apostome ciliates", peritrich = "Peritrich ciliates")
inf <- join_data %>%
  select(sample_id, site_code, season, clade, ctmax, size, paste0(names(inf_groups), "_call")) %>%
  pivot_longer(ends_with("_call"), names_to = "group", values_to = "positive",
               names_pattern = "(.*)_call") %>%
  mutate(collection = paste(site_code, season)) %>%
  group_by(group, collection) %>%
  filter(sum(positive) >= 2, sum(!positive) >= 2) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(group = factor(inf_groups[group], levels = inf_groups),
         status = factor(if_else(positive, "positive", "negative"), levels = c("negative", "positive")))

if (nrow(inf) == 0) {
  cat("No collection has both infected and uninfected individuals.")
} else {
  inf %>%
    pivot_longer(c(ctmax, size), names_to = "trait") %>%
    mutate(trait = recode(trait, ctmax = "CTmax (°C)", size = "Prosome length (mm)")) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = collection, y = value, colour = status)) +
    facet_grid(trait ~ group, scales = "free", space = "free_x",
               labeller = labeller(group = label_wrap_gen(12))) +
    geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.6),
               size = 1.8, alpha = 0.8) +
    stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 95, size = 10,
                 position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(negative = "grey65", positive = "grey10")) +
    labs(x = "Collection (site, season)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
    theme_matt_facets(base_size = 13) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: infection-models
infection_fit <- function(var) {
  d <- join_data %>%
    mutate(collection = paste(site_code, season), status = .data[[var]]) %>%
    group_by(collection) %>% filter(any(status), any(!status)) %>% ungroup()
  if (nrow(d) == 0) return(NULL)
  map_dfr(c("ctmax", "size"), function(tr) {
    m <- lme4::lmer(as.formula(paste(tr, "~ status + clade + (1 | collection)")), data = d)
    co <- summary(m)$coefficients["statusTRUE", ]
    tibble(covariate = var, trait = tr, n_collections = n_distinct(d$collection),
           n_positive = sum(d$status), effect = co[["Estimate"]], se = co[["Std. Error"]])
  })
}
bind_rows(infection_fit("parasite_any"), infection_fit("epibiont_any")) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "Effect of carrying a parasite or epibiont on CTmax and size, within collections (trait ~ status + clade + (1 | collection)); only collections with both positive and negative individuals.")
```

## 5. Partitioning vulnerability

Our study examines spatial and temporal variation in upper thermal limits for field-acclimated individuals. Given the short generation time of these copepods, our results likely reflect the combined influence of phenotypic plasticity (acclimation to the changes in temperature), local adaptation (variation amongst the sites), and genetic variation between the clades.

The four clades, while morphologically difficult to differentiate, have distinct geographic distributions and physiological tolerances. The inclusion of this clade-level variation decreases the slope of the CTmax vs. temperature regression. Ignoring this source of variation would lead to an overestimated capacity for *A. tonsa* to respond to warming (either through acclimation or via gene flow and evolutionary rescue).

```{r}
#| label: clade-trait-lat
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
join_data %>% 
  drop_na(clade) %>% 
  filter(clade != "A_hudsonica") %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = collection_temp, y = ctmax, colour = clade)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.3) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", linewidth = 2.5) + 
  geom_smooth(data = filter(join_data, clade != "A_hudsonica"),
              method = "lm", linewidth = 2.5, 
              colour = "black") + 
  labs(x = "Collection Temp. (°C)", 
       y = "CTmax (°C)") + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = clade_cols) + 
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

We illustrate the effects of these different levels of variation by calculating warming tolerance for each collection (site x collection temperature combination) under three different scenarios.

### Scenario 1 (Fixed CTmax)

Warming tolerance was calculated using the average CTmax from the peak season collections (across all sites and individuals regardless of clade). This essentially assumes a fixed CTmax that is constant across the geographic range examined.

```{r}
illus_data = join_data %>% 
  drop_na(clade) %>% 
  filter(clade != "A_hudsonica")

peak_mean = illus_data %>% 
  filter(season == "peak") %>% 
  summarise(mean = mean(ctmax))

mean_ctmax = peak_mean$mean[1]

mean_ctmax_profiles = temp_profiles %>% 
  group_by(region, doy) %>% 
  mutate("pred_wt" = mean_ctmax - temp_c) %>% 
  mutate(comparison = "Fixed CTmax") %>%  
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(region = fct_relevel(region, "Florida", "Chesapeake", "Connecticut",
                              "Maine", "Shediac", "Miramichi"))

```

### Scenario 2 (Clade-level variation)

Here, the same approach is taken but for each clade separately. The average CTmax from the peak season for each clade was used as a fixed CTmax value when calculating warming tolerance.

```{r}

clade_peak_mean = illus_data %>% 
  filter(season == "peak") %>% 
  group_by(clade) %>% 
  summarise(mean = mean(ctmax))


clade_mean_profiles = temp_profiles %>% 
  group_by(region, doy) %>% 
  mutate("F_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[1] - temp_c,
         "IV_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[2] - temp_c,
         "S_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[3] - temp_c,
         "X_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[4] - temp_c) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = c(F_wt, IV_wt, S_wt, X_wt), 
               names_to = "clade", 
               values_to = "pred_wt") %>% 
  mutate(clade = str_split_fixed(clade, pattern = "_", n = 2)[,1]) %>% 
  mutate(comparison = "Clade") %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(region = fct_relevel(region, "Florida", "Chesapeake", "Connecticut",
                              "Maine", "Shediac", "Miramichi"))

ggplot(clade_mean_profiles, aes(x = pred_wt, y = region, fill = region)) + 
  facet_wrap(clade~.) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + 
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(stat = "binline", bins = floor(max(clade_mean_profiles$pred_wt))) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = region_cols) +
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

### Scenario 3 (Clade variation and acclimation/adaptation)

Here CTmax is predicted based on the continuous temperature data and a model of CTmax as a function of the interaction between collection temperature and clade. The predicted CTmax values fall within the range of CTmax values observed in the field.

```{r}

pred.model = lm(data = illus_data, ctmax ~ collection_temp * clade)

pred_data = temp_profiles %>% 
  group_by(region, doy) %>% 
  mutate("F_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[1] - temp_c,
         "IV_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[2] - temp_c,
         "S_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[3] - temp_c,
         "X_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[4] - temp_c) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = c(F_wt, IV_wt, S_wt, X_wt), 
               names_to = "clade", 
               values_to = "pred_wt") %>% 
  mutate(clade = str_split_fixed(clade, pattern = "_", n = 2)[,1]) %>%  
  select(region, doy, date, "collection_temp" = temp_c, clade)


pred_data$pred_ctmax = predict(pred.model, newdata = pred_data)

full_pred_profiles = pred_data %>% 
  mutate(pred_wt = pred_ctmax - collection_temp) %>% 
  select(region, doy, date, "temp_c" = collection_temp, -pred_ctmax, clade, pred_wt) %>% 
  mutate(comparison = "Genetic Variation & Acclimation") %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(region = fct_relevel(region, "Florida", "Chesapeake", "Connecticut",
                              "Maine", "Shediac", "Miramichi"))

ggplot(full_pred_profiles, aes(x = pred_wt, y = region, fill = region)) + 
  facet_wrap(clade~.) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + 
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(stat = "binline", bins = floor(max(full_pred_profiles$pred_wt))) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = region_cols) +
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

### Comparing Scenarios

There is strong geographic variation in the distributions of these clades. It does not, for example, make sense to examine warming tolerance of Clade X individuals in Florida, as this clade was not collected from lower latitudes. To incorporate this distribution information, simulated populations were re-assembled reflecting the proportional clade composition within each region (calculated across the entire set of collections).

```{r}
#| label: region-clade-props
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 7
# First step is to generate a population of 100 individuals for each region reflecting the number of individuals in each clade 

pred_samples = illus_data %>%  
  mutate(region = case_when(
    site_code %in% c("MR", "FH") ~ "Florida",
    site_code %in% c("GW", "MD") ~ "Chesapeake",
    site_code == "CT" ~ "Connecticut",
    site_code == "ME" ~ "Maine",
    site_code == "TK" ~ "Shediac",
    site_code == "RW" ~ "Miramichi"
  )) %>% 
  group_by(region) %>%  
  count(clade) %>%
  ungroup() %>% 
  complete(region, clade, fill = list(n = 0)) %>% 
  group_by(region) %>% 
  mutate(total = sum(n)) %>% 
  group_by(region, clade) %>% 
  mutate(prop = n / total, 
         sample_size = round(prop * 100)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(region = fct_relevel(region, "Florida", "Chesapeake","Connecticut", "Maine", "Shediac", "Miramichi"))

ggplot(mutate(pred_samples, clade = factor(clade, levels = tonsa_clades)), aes(x = region, y = prop, fill = clade)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = clade_cols) + 
  labs(x = "Region", 
       y = "Proportion") + 
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "right")

```

Warming tolerance profiles for each clade were added in these proportions to generation populations of 100 individuals.

```{r}
clade_mean_populations = data.frame()
for(i in 1:dim(pred_samples)[1]){
  
  sub_region = pred_samples$region[i]
  sub_clade = pred_samples$clade[i]
  sample_size = pred_samples$sample_size[i]
  
  sub_data = clade_mean_profiles %>%  
    filter(region == sub_region,
           clade == sub_clade)
  
  #print(c(sub_region, sub_clade))
  
  new_df <- map(seq_len(sample_size),~sub_data) %>% 
    bind_rows() %>%  
    mutate("warming" = "no")
  
  clade_mean_populations = bind_rows(clade_mean_populations, new_df)
  
}

full_pred_populations = data.frame()
for(i in 1:dim(pred_samples)[1]){
  
  sub_region = pred_samples$region[i]
  sub_clade = pred_samples$clade[i]
  sample_size = pred_samples$sample_size[i]
  
  sub_data = full_pred_profiles %>%  
    filter(region == sub_region,
           clade == sub_clade)
  
  #print(c(sub_region, sub_clade))
  
  new_df <- map(seq_len(sample_size),~sub_data) %>% 
    bind_rows() %>%  
    mutate("warming" = "no")
  
  full_pred_populations = bind_rows(full_pred_populations, new_df)
  
}

```

The warming tolerance distributions for each region and the three different scenarios are shown below.

```{r}
#| label: peak-season-wt

current_mean_ctmax_plot = ggplot(mean_ctmax_profiles, aes(x = pred_wt, y = region, fill = region)) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(5, 15, 25, 35), colour = "grey") + 
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(stat = "binline", bins = floor(max(mean_ctmax_profiles$pred_wt))) + 
  xlim(-5,40) + 
  labs(x = "Predicted Warming Tolerance (°C)", 
       y = "Region", 
       title = "Overall Mean") + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = region_cols) +
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")


current_clade_mean_plot = ggplot(clade_mean_populations, aes(x = pred_wt, y = region, fill = region)) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(5, 15, 25, 35), colour = "grey") + 
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(stat = "binline", bins = floor(max(clade_mean_populations$pred_wt))) + 
  xlim(-5, 40) + 
  labs(x = "Predicted Warming Tolerance (°C)", 
       y = "Region", 
       title = "Clade Means") + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = region_cols) +
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")


current_full_pred_plot = ggplot(full_pred_populations, aes(x = pred_wt, y = region, fill = region)) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(5, 15, 25, 35), colour = "grey") + 
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(stat = "binline", bins = floor(max(full_pred_populations$pred_wt))) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = region_cols) +
  xlim(-5, 40)  + 
  labs(x = "Predicted Warming Tolerance (°C)", 
       y = "Region", 
       title = "Full Prediction") + 
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")

ggarrange(current_mean_ctmax_plot, current_clade_mean_plot, current_full_pred_plot, 
          nrow = 3, labels = "AUTO")
```

Overall, differences were fairly minor, with slight increases in predicted warming tolerance in low latitude regions and slight decreases in higher latitude regions.

We also examined potential effects of warming (a +4°C increase in temperature). These predictions assume clade composition does not change over time and that warming is constant throughout the year.

```{r}

warming_clade_mean_profiles = temp_profiles %>% 
  mutate(temp_c = temp_c + 4) %>% 
  group_by(region, doy) %>% 
  mutate("F_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[1] - temp_c,
         "IV_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[2] - temp_c,
         "S_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[3] - temp_c,
         "X_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[4] - temp_c) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = c(F_wt, IV_wt, S_wt, X_wt), 
               names_to = "clade", 
               values_to = "pred_wt") %>% 
  mutate(clade = str_split_fixed(clade, pattern = "_", n = 2)[,1]) %>% 
  mutate(comparison = "Clade") %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(region = fct_relevel(region, "Florida", "Chesapeake", "Connecticut",
                              "Maine", "Shediac", "Miramichi"))

warming_clade_mean_populations = data.frame()
for(i in 1:dim(pred_samples)[1]){
  
  sub_region = pred_samples$region[i]
  sub_clade = pred_samples$clade[i]
  sample_size = pred_samples$sample_size[i]
  
  sub_data = warming_clade_mean_profiles %>%  
    filter(region == sub_region,
           clade == sub_clade)
  
  #print(c(sub_region, sub_clade))
  
  new_df <- map(seq_len(sample_size),~sub_data) %>% 
    bind_rows() %>%  
    mutate("warming" = "yes")
  
  warming_clade_mean_populations = bind_rows(warming_clade_mean_populations, new_df)
  
}


warming_pred_data = temp_profiles %>% 
  mutate(temp_c = temp_c + 4) %>% 
  group_by(region, doy) %>% 
  mutate("F_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[1] - temp_c,
         "IV_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[2] - temp_c,
         "S_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[3] - temp_c,
         "X_wt" = clade_peak_mean$mean[4] - temp_c) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = c(F_wt, IV_wt, S_wt, X_wt), 
               names_to = "clade", 
               values_to = "pred_wt") %>% 
  mutate(clade = str_split_fixed(clade, pattern = "_", n = 2)[,1]) %>%  
  select(region, doy, date, "collection_temp" = temp_c, clade)


warming_pred_data$pred_ctmax = predict(pred.model, newdata = warming_pred_data)

warming_full_pred_profiles = warming_pred_data %>% 
  mutate(pred_wt = pred_ctmax - collection_temp) %>% 
  select(region, doy, date, "temp_c" = collection_temp, -pred_ctmax, clade, pred_wt) %>% 
  mutate(comparison = "Genetic Variation & Acclimation") %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(region = fct_relevel(region, "Florida", "Chesapeake", "Connecticut",
                              "Maine", "Shediac", "Miramichi"))


warming_full_pred_populations = data.frame()
for(i in 1:dim(pred_samples)[1]){
  
  sub_region = pred_samples$region[i]
  sub_clade = pred_samples$clade[i]
  sample_size = pred_samples$sample_size[i]
  
  sub_data = warming_full_pred_profiles %>%  
    filter(region == sub_region,
           clade == sub_clade)
  
  #print(c(sub_region, sub_clade))
  
  new_df <- map(seq_len(sample_size),~sub_data) %>% 
    bind_rows() %>%  
    mutate("warming" = "yes")
  
  warming_full_pred_populations = bind_rows(warming_full_pred_populations, new_df)
  
}

### Show as histogram ridges with different alphas? Or different shades of the ssame region colors

```

Unsurprisingly warming decreases the predicted warming tolerance. Similar patterns are observed as in the comparison between the initial three scenarios - predicted warming tolerance under warming is lowest in Florida and highest in the high latitude regions. Similarly, including clade-level variation and acclimation increases warming tolerance in the lower latitude regions and decreases it in the higher latitude regions.


To simplify the comparisons, here we subset the data to just August and September (the warmest months and the season typically associated with the highest abundance of A. tonsa).

```{r}
#| label: wt-range-scenarios
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8

wt_comps = bind_rows(mean_ctmax_profiles %>% 
  mutate(warming = "no") %>% 
  bind_rows(warming_mean_ctmax_profiles),
clade_mean_populations, 
warming_clade_mean_populations, 
full_pred_populations, 
warming_full_pred_populations) %>% 
  group_by(region, comparison, warming) %>% 
  summarise(mean_wt = mean(pred_wt),
            min_wt = min(pred_wt),
            max_wt = max(pred_wt)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(comparison = fct_relevel(comparison, "Fixed CTmax", "Genetic Variation", "Genetic Variation & Acclimation"))

peak_comps = bind_rows(mean_ctmax_profiles %>% 
  mutate(warming = "no") %>% 
  bind_rows(warming_mean_ctmax_profiles),
clade_mean_populations, 
warming_clade_mean_populations, 
full_pred_populations, 
warming_full_pred_populations) %>% 
  mutate("month" = month(date)) %>% 
  filter(month %in% c(8,9)) %>%  
  group_by(region, comparison, warming) %>% 
  summarise(mean_wt = mean(pred_wt),
            min_wt = min(pred_wt),
            max_wt = max(pred_wt)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(comparison = fct_relevel(comparison, "Fixed CTmax", "Genetic Variation", "Genetic Variation & Acclimation"))

ggplot(peak_comps, aes(x = comparison, y = mean_wt, colour = warming, group = warming))+ 
  facet_wrap(region~., 
             nrow = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + 
  geom_point(size = 3,
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.3)) + 
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = min_wt, ymax = max_wt),
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.3),
                width = 0.1, linewidth = 1) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5,
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.3)) + 
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("no" = "darkslategray", 
                                 "yes" = "darksalmon")) + 
  labs(x = "", 
       y = "Warming Tolerance (°C)") + 
  theme_matt_facets() + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 300, hjust = 0, vjust = 0.5))

```

Changes were slight between the scenarios, with the same relative patterns between the current and warming scenarios. Compared to the fixed CTmax estimate, incorporating both genetic diversity and acclimation reduced the range of warming tolerance estimates across the samples by \~30%.

```{r}

range_changes = wt_comps %>%  
  filter(warming == "no") %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  group_by(warming, comparison) %>% 
  summarise(wt_range = max(min_wt) - min(min_wt)) %>% 
  mutate(percent_decrease = 100 * (1 - (wt_range / wt_range[1]))) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  select("Comparison" = comparison, "WT Range" = wt_range, "% Decrease" = percent_decrease) %>% 
  arrange(`% Decrease`)
 
# Saved for the phenotype manuscript (Table 2)
write.csv(range_changes, file = here("Output", "Output_data", "range_changes.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

knitr::kable(range_changes, digits = 2)

```
